According to the Indian Journal of Pediatrics (Padmanabha et al., 2019), home-based systematic instruction with planned prompt fading showed significant functional independence gains within 8–12 weeks — in Indian family contexts, by Indian caregivers. DOI: 10.1007/s12098-018-2747-4
The Neuroscience of "Waiting for Help"
What's Actually Happening
When a child receives a prompt before attempting a task independently, the brain associates the antecedent stimulus (the task) with the prompt — not with the correct response. Over repeated trials, the brain builds a neural pathway that routes: See task → Wait for prompt → Respond.
This is stimulus control transfer — a well-documented phenomenon in behavioural neuroscience. The prompt becomes the discriminative stimulus (SD) that "signals" the response. The task alone does not.
Brain regions involved:
  • Prefrontal cortex (executive initiation)
  • Basal ganglia (habit formation pathways)
  • Cerebellum (motor sequence learning)
What This Means for You
Your child's brain has learned: "When I see a task, I wait for mum's cue — because the cue always comes and the cue means success."
This is not stubbornness. It is not manipulation. It is efficient neural wiring — your child learned exactly what the environment taught.
The good news: the same brain plasticity that created prompt dependency can reverse it. Systematic prompt fading rewires the pathway from task → wait to task → respond.
"This is a wiring pattern, not a character flaw. And wiring can be changed." — Pinnacle Consortium, NeuroDev + ABA Integration
Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020): DOI: 10.3389/fnint.2020.556660
Your Child's Learning Journey — Where Prompting Fits
Understanding where systematic prompting fits within the broader arc of development helps caregivers and clinicians set realistic expectations and make informed decisions about when and how to intervene.
1
Age 0–2
Natural Scaffolding — caregiver naturally helps
2
Age 2–4
Intentional Prompting — skill-specific prompting begins
3
Age 4–7
Systematic Prompt Fading — data-driven fading begins
4
Age 7–12
Fading to Natural Cues — independence across settings
5
Age 12+
Self-Management — self-prompting strategies
Typical Development
  • Natural scaffolding fades intuitively
  • Child initiates as competence grows
  • Parent naturally gives less help over time
  • Errors motivate independent attempts
With Developmental Differences
  • Scaffolding must be faded intentionally
  • Initiation may need explicit teaching
  • Parent needs a systematic fading plan
  • Errors may increase avoidance

Prompting & Prompt Hierarchy: The Formal Definition
ABA/BCBA
Systematic Instruction
All Ages 2+
All Settings
8–12 Week Outcomes

Formal Definition:Prompting is any assistance — physical, gestural, visual, verbal, or modelled — given to help a learner perform a behaviour or skill they cannot yet do independently. A Prompt Hierarchy is the structured sequence of prompt types arranged from most intrusive (full physical guidance) to least intrusive (independent), used to systematically plan and fade support toward independence.
🟣"The Bridge System" — Building the bridge from 'can't do it yet' to 'doing it alone.'
Enables Success
Every trial ends correctly — building confidence and neural pathways
Builds Independence
Systematic fading ensures prompts shrink as competence grows
Prevents Dependency
A fading plan prevents help from becoming a permanent crutch
Who Uses It
  • ABA/BCBA → primary systematic prompting design and data systems
  • OT → motor skill prompting, hand-over-hand guidance
  • SLP → communication prompting, verbal script fading
  • SpEd → academic skill prompting, classroom visual supports
Adjacent Techniques
  • L-928: Shaping
  • L-930: Reinforcement
  • L-931: Generalisation
  • L-932: Maintenance
The Whole Consortium Uses Prompting — Here's How Each Discipline Applies It
ABA / BCBA — Primary Lead
Designs the prompt hierarchy, selects prompt types for each skill, writes formal fading protocols, sets mastery criteria, supervises data collection. The BCBA holds the "system" view — ensuring every skill has a prompt plan and a fading plan.
Occupational Therapy
Applies physical prompting for motor tasks: hand-over-hand for pencil grip, feeding utensils, dressing sequences. Specialises in graduated physical guidance — knowing how much physical support the sensory system can tolerate while building motor patterns.
Speech-Language Pathology
Designs verbal prompt scripts for communication skills: "Say 'more'" → "Mo—" → expectant pause → independent initiation. Manages the subtle art of fading language cues without losing the communication attempt.
Special Education
Implements visual and gestural prompts in academic settings: pointing to the correct line, colour-coded answer choices, picture cue sequences. Coordinates multi-prompter consistency across classroom staff.

"The brain does not organise by therapy type. A prompting strategy that works for OT's motor sequence will use the same fading principles as ABA's verbal skill protocol. This is why we train as one consortium — because your child needs one coherent prompting language across everyone who works with them." — Pinnacle Blooms Consortium Integration Protocol
What Skills Does Systematic Prompting Build?
Prompting is not a technique for a specific skill — it is the delivery mechanism for teaching any skill. Every skill your child needs to develop can be taught more effectively with the right prompting approach. Here are the primary skill domains where systematic prompting delivers the strongest outcomes.
Self-Care & Daily Living
Dressing sequences, tooth brushing steps, handwashing, toileting independence, feeding with utensils, hair management. Most common area for prompt dependency — and most impactful when independence is achieved.
Communication & Language
Requesting preferred items, labelling objects and actions, social greetings, answering questions, initiating conversations, script fading for social exchanges.
Academic & Cognitive Skills
Writing letter sequences, reading comprehension steps, maths operation procedures, task completion without redirection, classroom routine following.
Play & Social Skills
Joining peer play, turn-taking sequences, game rule following, toy play with peers, cooperative activities.
Behavioural Routines
Transition following, schedule compliance, waiting behaviour, following multi-step instructions, emotional regulation sequences.

Material 01: Prompt Hierarchy Visual Charts
Canon Category: Visual Supports / Prompt Systems
📊The roadmap from full support to independence. The foundation of all systematic prompting. A visual chart displaying the complete hierarchy — Full Physical → Partial Physical → Model → Gestural → Verbal → Visual → Independent — gives everyone (parent, therapist, teacher) a shared language. When the hierarchy is visible, fading becomes trackable.
Commercial Options
  • Prompt Hierarchy Poster (laminated) — ₹150–500
  • Colour-coded prompt level tracker
  • Pocket reference card for school bag
₹0 DIY Version
Draw on A4 paper; laminate for durability. Mark current prompt level with a sticky dot. Move the dot as prompts fade. Post in therapy space AND at home. Same information — visibility = same function.
🔗Search Prompt Hierarchy Charts on Amazon.in
Material 02: Visual Prompts & Picture Cues
Canon Category: Visual Supports / Picture Communication
🖼️Support that stays when you step back. Visual prompts — picture sequences, arrows, highlighted choices, step-by-step photo cards — provide guidance without requiring another person to be present. They can remain in the environment and fade naturally: photo → line drawing → icon → removal.
Commercial Options — ₹100–400
  • Printed picture card sets
  • Task analysis photo strips
  • Arrow and choice-highlighting overlays
₹0 DIY Version
Photograph each step of the target task on your phone. Print or display on tablet. Use arrows cut from paper to point to correct choices. Photographs of your child's own environment are often more meaningful than stock images. Fully effective and completely free.
🔗Search Visual Prompt Cards on Amazon.in
Material 03: Gestural Prompt Training Cards
Canon Category: Behavioural Teaching Tools
👆The power of pointing, nodding, and looking. Gestural prompts — pointing, head nodding, eye gaze direction, tapping near a target — are powerful, subtle, and highly fade-able. Training cards help adults learn which gesture to use and how to fade: obvious point → subtle point → eye gaze → expectant waiting.
Obvious Point
Clear, extended finger pointing directly to target
Subtle Point
Brief, smaller gesture near the target area
Eye Gaze
Look toward the correct item without pointing
Expectant Waiting
Silent pause with open, anticipatory expression

₹0 DIY: Write or draw your gestural fading sequence on index cards. Practise with your co-caregiver. The gesture itself is free — the card helps you be consistent. Gestural prompts also work in public without drawing attention.
🔗Search Gestural Prompt Guide on Amazon.in
Material 04: Prompt Data Collection Forms
Canon Category: Data Tracking / Progress Monitoring
📋Track prompts so you know when to fade. Data collection transforms prompting from intuition to science. Recording what prompt level was used for each trial — and watching that level decrease over sessions — is the only way to know whether your fading plan is working. Without data, prompts get stuck.
Prompt Code Legend
  • FP — Full Physical (hand-over-hand)
  • PP — Partial Physical
  • M — Model
  • G — Gestural
  • V — Verbal
  • Vi — Visual
  • I — Independent
₹0 DIY System
Use a simple tally system: FP / PP / M / G / V / Vi / I. One row per session. Take 30 seconds to record after each skill practice. Review weekly. Track the number — not the paperwork. Price range: ₹100–300
🛒Reward Stickers for Tracking Charts — ₹364
Material 05: Model Prompts & Video Models
Canon Category: Visual Learning / Video Modelling
🎥Show, don't just tell. Model prompts show the complete target behaviour for the learner to imitate. Video modelling is especially powerful: the learner watches correct performance, then imitates. Videos can be replayed and used independently.
Live Model Prompts
Adult demonstrates the full correct behaviour. Child watches, then imitates. Requires adult presence each trial.
Video Modelling
Pre-recorded correct performance viewed on phone or tablet. Replayable. Works independently without adult present. Price range: ₹200–600.
Self-Modelling Videos ⭐
Film your child completing a skill successfully with assistance. Use that video as the model for future sessions. Self-modelling videos have the highest generalisation outcomes of all model types.

₹0 DIY: Your smartphone is your video model studio. Film, playback, repeat. NCAEP (2020) classifies video modelling as an Established Evidence-Based Practice for autism.
Material 06: Physical Prompt Guides (Hand-Over-Hand)
Canon Category: Motor Guidance / Physical Teaching Tools
🤝When and how to use hands-on help. Physical prompting — hand-over-hand, wrist guidance, elbow touch, shoulder cue, shadow hover — is the most supportive prompt type. Physical prompt guides teach adults the critical fading sequence.
Full Physical (Hand-over-Hand)
Complete guidance through entire motor pattern. Starting point for new motor skills.
Wrist / Elbow Guidance
Partial physical contact — guide from further from the action.
Shoulder Cue
Light touch at shoulder initiates movement. Minimal contact.
Shadow Hover
Hands near but not touching. Child moves independently.
Independent
No physical contact. Task alone triggers correct response.

Key Principle — Proximal to Distal Fading: Always move your guidance point away from the action toward the shoulder. Hover before removing completely. Price range: ₹150–400. ₹0 DIY: The guide is knowledge, not a purchased item — understanding this principle costs nothing.
Material 07: Verbal Prompt Scripts & Fading Guides
Canon Category: Communication Teaching Tools
💬Words that help, then fade away. Verbal prompts are the most overused and hardest to fade. Scripted prompts ensure consistency across all caregivers, and fading scripts show the clear path from full verbal support to independent communication.
Full Verbal
"Say 'ball'" — complete instruction delivered
Partial Verbal
"Ball" — partial model only
Phonemic Cue
"Ba—" — first sound only
Expectant Silence
[Pause] + expectant facial expression
Independent
Child initiates without any verbal cue

Rule: Always use LESS words first. Then add more only if needed. ₹0 DIY: Write your verbal prompt fading sequence on an index card for each target skill. Pin to the therapy wall. Train everyone who works with your child to use the same script at the same level. Price range: ₹100–300.
Material 08: Time Delay Materials
Canon Category: Systematic Teaching Tools / Timers
⏱️Wait before you prompt. Time delay — inserting 3–5 seconds of waiting between presenting a task and providing a prompt — is one of the most effective techniques for increasing independent responding. Most adults prompt too fast. The delay gives the brain a genuine chance to self-initiate.
Why It Works
The waiting interval creates a "response opportunity window." If the child responds during the delay — that's an independent response. The delay is where independence lives.
How to Implement
Count silently to 5 in your head before prompting. Or use the timer on your phone. Apply it every trial, consistently. The science is in the waiting, not the timer itself.
Progressive Time Delay
Start with 2 seconds; increase to 5 seconds as child builds tolerance. Track whether independent responses increase. If yes — the delay is working.
🛒Smartivity DIY Interactive Clock — ₹673(Canon: Number/Counting Materials — teaches time concepts alongside timing strategies)

₹0 DIY: Count silently to 5 in your head before prompting. Price range: ₹100–300. 📞 Free Helpline: 9100 181 181
Material 09: Prompt Fading Decision Trees & Mastery Criteria
Canon Category: Clinical Decision Tools / Planning Materials
🌳Know when to give less help. Decision trees answer the question every parent and therapist struggles with: When is it time to fade? Mastery criteria define the threshold that triggers the next level of fading — removing guesswork from the most critical moment in skill teaching.
The Mastery Criteria Formula
Write your mastery criteria on paper:
"If [child] responds correctly [4 out of 5 times] at [current prompt level] for [2 sessions in a row] → fade to next level."
Post it. Follow it. This single rule prevents prompt dependency from forming.
Without Decision Rules
Fading is guesswork. Prompts stay too long. Dependency deepens. The child learns that the current level of help is "normal." The mastery criteria are the mechanism that keeps the system moving forward — automatically.
Price range: ₹100–300 | ₹0 DIY: Written criteria on paper

Before You Begin: Safety & Contraindications

🔴RED LINE — STOP: DO NOT PROCEED IF:
• Your child shows significant distress or self-injurious behaviour when prompts are removed
• Your child has active medical issues (illness, medication change, sleep deprivation) — reschedule
• Physical prompting causes obvious pain, extreme resistance, or panic — consult OT immediately
• You have no plan for what to do when the child makes an error — errors without a correction plan can entrench incorrect patterns
• Multiple adults are giving completely different prompt levels for the same skill — inconsistency causes more harm than no prompting at all

🟡AMBER — MODIFY IF:
• Child has tactile defensiveness — consult OT before using physical prompts; start with gestural or visual
• Child is tired, hungry, or post-meltdown — use simplified version only or postpone
• Child shows signs of prompt fatigue (turning away, pushing materials) — take a break; resume in 30 minutes
• You are uncertain about which prompt level to use — start with least-to-most hierarchy

🟢GREEN — PROCEED WHEN:
• Child is fed, rested, and in a regulated state
• You have your prompt hierarchy written and visible
• You have decided which prompt type to use for today's target skill
• You have a data sheet ready (or tally system in head)
• Your fading plan is decided: "If [child] does X correctly Y times, I'll use less help next session"
• All caregivers in the session know today's prompt level

📞Pinnacle FREE Helpline: 9100 181 181
If you are unsure whether to proceed, call us. Our BCBA consultants can guide you through a safety assessment in real time — at no cost.
Prepare Your Space Before You Begin
A well-organised environment is not a luxury — it is a clinical variable. The physical setup of your learning space directly affects the quality of prompt delivery, the child's ability to attend, and your own capacity to follow the hierarchy consistently.
Remove From the Space
  • Unrelated toys or distracting items
  • Screen devices (TV, phone visible to child)
  • Other people who aren't part of this session
Arrange
  • Materials laid out in task order (left to right)
  • Prompt hierarchy chart visible to you and child
  • Reinforcement item available but not immediately accessible
  • Timer ready (phone timer or visual timer)
  • Data sheet on clipboard beside you
Environment Checklist
  • Lighting: bright and even (no harsh shadows on materials)
  • Sound: quiet — close doors; pause TV
  • Temperature: comfortable for child
  • Duration planned: 10–20 minutes maximum for structured sessions
  • Reinforcer confirmed effective today
  • Prompt hierarchy visible at child eye-level

Spatial Principle: Parent behind or beside — never across. Physical proximity enables prompting. Cross-table positioning slows physical and gestural prompt delivery and increases the child's opportunity to avoid. PMC10955541 — structured environment effect on session efficacy.
60-Second Pre-Session Readiness Check
Physical Readiness
  • Child has eaten within the last 2 hours
  • Child has had adequate sleep last night
  • No signs of illness (fever, pain, unusual fatigue)
  • Child has had physical movement/break before session
Emotional / Behavioural Readiness
  • No meltdown or significant distress in last 30 minutes
  • Child is not currently in heightened sensory state
  • Child is not perseverating on an unrelated topic or object
Environmental Readiness
  • Space is set up per the setup guidelines
  • You have 15–20 uninterrupted minutes
  • Reinforcer is ready and known to be effective today
✅ All Green
PROCEED to full session
⚠️ 3–5 Amber
MODIFY: Shorter session, simpler skill, more support
❌ 2+ Red
POSTPONE: Do a calming activity instead. Try tomorrow.

If Postpone — Do This Instead: Choose a preferred activity with NO demands. No prompting, no teaching. Just connection. A day without a session is not a lost day — a session started wrong can set back weeks of progress.
Step 1: The Invitation
① THE INVITATION
30–60 seconds
ACT III: The Execution
Say: "Hey [child's name], come sit with me — I have something fun for us."

Do NOT say: "It's time for therapy." / "Come practise." / "We need to work on ___."
Why: Demand-free entry reduces resistance before the session begins. The brain needs to associate the learning space with positive anticipation — not obligation.
Body Language Guide
  • 🟣Face: Warm, genuine smile. Not forced enthusiasm.
  • 🟣Body: Open posture, leaning slightly toward child
  • 🟣Voice: Calm, inviting — medium volume
  • 🟣Position: At child's level if possible
What Acceptance Looks Like
  • ✅ Child moves toward you / the table
  • ✅ Child makes eye contact or looks at the materials
  • ✅ Child picks up a material out of curiosity
  • ✅ Child sits (even with fidgeting)
If There Is Resistance
  • Child moves away → Give 30 more seconds; try showing the reinforcer
  • Child ignores → Approach gently; place one material in front casually
  • Child protests → "I hear you. Just one thing, then [preferred activity]."

ABA Pairing Principle: The therapist/parent must become a conditioned reinforcer before introducing demands. The Invitation is pairing in action.
Step 2: The Engagement
② THE ENGAGEMENT
1–3 minutes
The child is now present. This step introduces the material or activity — but NOT the demand yet. You are building motivation before instruction begins.
Script for Material Introduction:
"Look at this — [show material/task]. Want to try? Watch me first."
(Model the first step yourself with exaggerated clarity)
Before presenting any demand, decide which prompt level you're using for this skill today. This is your starting point on the hierarchy.

This Means...

Leaning in, reaching
High engagement
Introduce the demand now
Watching but not moving
Moderate engagement
Give one more model; then invite participation
Looking away occasionally
Low engagement
Use a preferred material version; simplify the task
Turning away
Disengaged
Return to Invitation phase; reduce demand level

When child shows engagement, immediately deliver specific verbal reinforcement: "Great — you're watching! I love that." Reinforce the engagement itself, before any correct response.
Step 3: The Therapeutic Action — Choosing Your Hierarchy Direction
③ THE THERAPEUTIC ACTION
5–15 minutes
Option A: Most-to-Least
For new skills or errorless learning
  1. Present the task/SD clearly
  1. Immediately deliver the planned prompt
  1. Child responds correctly (because you prompted correctly)
  1. Deliver reinforcement: "Yes! [Specific praise]!"
  1. Record: prompt level used + Correct ✓
  1. Repeat 3–5 trials at same prompt level
  1. If 4/5 correct → begin fading one level down next set
Option B: Least-to-Most
For skills partially in repertoire
  1. Present the task/SD clearly
  1. WAIT — count silently to 4–5 seconds (Time Delay)
  1. Independent correct response → reinforce enthusiastically + record: I ✓✓✓
  1. No response or error → deliver LEAST intrusive prompt first
  1. Correct with minimal prompt → reinforce + record prompt level
  1. Still no response → move up one level on the hierarchy
  1. Ensure every trial ends in correct response
Step 3 (Continued): Prompt Type Execution Guide
🤝 Full Physical (Hand-over-Hand)
Position: Behind or beside child; never across. Guidance: Full hand-over-hand through entire motor pattern. Pressure: Firm enough to guide; gentle enough to follow. Fade signal: Child begins moving in correct direction without your full pressure. Next step: Reduce to partial physical (wrist or elbow guidance only).
👋 Gestural (Point / Nod / Eye Gaze)
Types: Direct point → Indirect point → Head nod → Eye gaze → Expectant look. Fade: Make gesture progressively subtler over trials. Community use: Gestural prompts work in public without drawing attention.
🗣️ Verbal
Full verbal: "Put the cup on the shelf." Partial verbal: "Put the cup on the ___." Phonemic: "Sh___" (first sound). Expectant pause: [silence] + expectant facial expression. Rule: Always use LESS words first. Then add more only if needed.
🖼️ Visual
Position visual cue at child's eye level and within arm's reach. Fade: Picture → line drawing → icon → removal. Visual prompts do not require adult presence — this is their power.
Step 4: Reinforcement
④ REINFORCEMENT
Every Correct Trial
Every correct response — regardless of prompt level — must be followed immediately by reinforcement. The goal of reinforcement during prompting is to build the association between the behaviour (not the prompt) and the reward.
Verbal Reinforcement (Always Present)
  • "Yes! You did it!" ← specific, immediate, genuine
  • "That's exactly right — you put it there!" ← describe the behaviour
  • "Good boy/girl" — too vague for learning association
Differential Reinforcement (Critical)
Deliver MORE enthusiastic/valuable reinforcement for independent (unprompted) responses. This teaches the child that independence is more rewarding than waiting for prompts.
  • Independent response → ⭐⭐⭐ BIG reinforcement + specific praise
  • Gestural prompt → ⭐⭐ Good reinforcement + specific praise
  • Verbal prompt → ⭐ Reinforcement + encouragement
  • Physical prompt → ✓ Reinforcement (minimum — ensure positive)

🛒Reward Jar — ₹589 | 🛒1800+ Reward Stickers — ₹364
📞FREE Helpline: 9100 181 181 — Ask our BCBA about customising your child's reinforcement menu
Step 5: Cool-Down
⑤ COOL-DOWN
2–5 minutes
Every structured learning session must end with a preferred, non-demanding activity that leaves the child's nervous system in a positive state. This ensures the child associates the learning space with positive outcomes — which makes the next session easier to begin.
Transition Signal
Give a transition signal 2 minutes before ending: "Two more tries, then we're done — and then [preferred activity]."
Complete Final Trial
Finish the session on a correct, successful response whenever possible.
Celebrate the Session
"We did such good work today. I'm so proud of you."
Hand Over Preferred Item
Immediately — no delay, no conditions. Stay present for 2 minutes of free play with no demands.
Age
Max Session Duration
2–3 years
5–10 minutes
4–6 years
10–15 minutes
7–10 years
15–20 minutes
10+ years
20–30 minutes

❌ Do not end abruptly without transition warning. ❌ Do not use cool-down time to "squeeze in one more." ❌ Do not withhold the preferred item if the session was difficult. ❌ Do not debrief or correct the child about errors during cool-down.
Track Prompts So You Know When to Fade
"You can't fade what you don't track." — Pinnacle ABA Consortium. Without data, prompting becomes intuitive — and intuition maintains prompts longer than necessary. Data answers the only question that matters: Is the prompt level decreasing over time?

Fading Decision Rule — Post This on Your Wall:
If: 80% correct at current prompt level across 2–3 consecutive sessions
Then: Fade to the next level down the hierarchy

When Prompting Isn't Producing Progress: Diagnostic Guide
1
Problem 01: "She still waits for my cue no matter what I do"
Likely Cause: Prompt delivered before child has a chance to initiate independently (no time delay built in)
Solution: Use the 4–5 second time delay BEFORE any prompt. Count silently. Let the opportunity exist before filling it.
2
Problem 02: "When I reduce the prompt level, he just fails"
Likely Cause: Fading too fast — mastery criteria not met at current level, OR gap between levels is too large
Solution: Return to previous level for 2–3 more sessions. Then try a smaller fade (e.g., full verbal to partial verbal, not all the way to gestural).
3
Problem 03: "She does it with me but not with her therapist / teacher"
Likely Cause: Skill is person-specific, not generalised — she learned with you as the prompt, not the task as the trigger
Solution: Vary prompters systematically. Dad prompts one session. Grandparent the next. Therapist the next.
4
Problem 04: "Different people in our house give different amounts of help"
Likely Cause: No shared prompt plan — everyone is responding to the moment, not following a hierarchy
Solution: Write current prompt level for each skill on the data sheet. Post it. Everyone follows the same plan.
5
Problem 05: "My child gets frustrated and shuts down when I try to give less help"
Likely Cause: Error rate is too high after fading, OR reinforcement for independent attempts is insufficient
Solution: Increase differential reinforcement — make independent attempts MORE rewarding than prompted ones. Consider most-to-least (errorless) approach.

📞9100 181 181 — BCBA support available for persistent prompting challenges
Personalising the Prompting Approach for Your Child
No two children are the same. Effective prompting requires adapting the hierarchy to your child's sensory profile, communication level, and age. Use the adaptation guide below to tailor your approach.
By Sensory Profile
  • Tactile-defensive: Minimise physical prompts; prioritise gestural and visual. Consult OT before any hand-over-hand.
  • Auditory-sensitive: Reduce verbal prompts; use more visual. Speak softer. Consider silent gestural-only sessions.
  • Visual thinker: Maximise visual prompt system — photos, task analysis cards, visual decision trees.
  • Sensory seeker: Use brief physical prompts (they may welcome the input). Channel seeking into correct response.
By Communication Profile
  • No verbal communication: Visual + Gestural primary; Physical for motor tasks; Avoid verbal as main channel.
  • Emerging verbal: Verbal partial prompts (phonemic) + Visual supports.
  • Functional verbal: Verbal + Gestural + Time delay; minimal physical.
  • Heavy echolalia: Reduce verbal model prompts; use more visual/gestural to avoid echolalic responses.
By Age Group
  • 2–4 years: Fully naturalistic; embedding prompts in play; 5–8 minute maximum sessions.
  • 5–8 years: Structured sessions + natural generalisation moments; 10–15 minutes.
  • 9–12 years: Self-monitoring introduced; teach child to recognise prompt levels; 15–20 minutes.
  • Teen+: Self-management and self-prompting strategies; move toward independence planning.
Weeks 1–2: The Foundation Phase
ACT IV: The Progress Arc
Progress: 15%
What You Will Likely See
  • ✅ Child begins to anticipate the session (approaches table without resistance)
  • ✅Slightly faster response after prompt delivery (latency decreasing)
  • ✅ Child shows increased tolerance for the prompt — less resistance to physical guidance
  • ✅ You feel more systematic — you're using the hierarchy, not improvising
What You Won't See Yet (That's Normal)
  • ❌ Independent responses without prompts — too early
  • ❌ Generalisation to other settings — that comes in weeks 5–8
  • ❌ Consistent same-prompt-level success — variability is expected in weeks 1–2
"If your child tolerates the gestural prompt when they used to need verbal — that IS progress. If they respond correctly 3 out of 5 times this week versus 1 out of 5 last week — that IS progress. The bar in weeks 1–2 is tolerance and consistency, not independence."
PMC11506176 — 8–12 week intervention outcome timelines
Weeks 3–4: Neural Pathways Forming
ACT IV: The Progress Arc
Progress: 40%
Consolidation Indicators
  • ✅ Child responds at a lower prompt level consistently (e.g., gestural instead of verbal)
  • ✅Response latency is noticeably shorter — child is anticipating
  • ✅ Child occasionally self-initiates before the prompt is delivered
  • ✅ Data shows clear downward trend in prompt level used
Subtle Signs of Neural Consolidation
These behaviours signal the brain is building the correct stimulus-response association:
  • Child reaches toward the correct item before you gesture
  • Child begins the sequence independently for the first 1–2 steps
  • Child uses the visual prompt without you directing them to it

When to Increase Frequency: If you're seeing consolidation signs — increase session frequency, not duration. Three 10-minute sessions are more effective than one 30-minute session. Repetition strengthens the pathway.

"In weeks 3–4, you may notice you're more confident too. You're no longer improvising — you're executing a system. That shift matters for your child, because your calm consistency communicates safety."
Weeks 5–8: Independence Begins to Emerge
ACT IV: The Progress Arc
Progress: 70%
What to Watch For
  • ✅ Child performs the skill independently in the training setting with minimal or no prompts
  • ✅ Skill begins appearing spontaneously in daily life (generalisation seeds)
  • ✅ Child corrects their own errors without adult intervention
  • ✅ Child shows pride and self-awareness about their own independence
The Generalisation Window
Weeks 5–8 is when you should deliberately introduce generalisation trials:
  • New setting: Kitchen table instead of therapy room
  • New prompter: Dad instead of Mum
  • New materials: Different coloured cup / different spoon
  • New time of day: Morning instead of evening

Your Fading Decisions Now: If 80% correct across 2–3 sessions at current level → move one level down. If errors reappear after fading → return one level; hold 3 more sessions. If stuck at same level for 3+ sessions → consult BCBA or call 9100 181 181.
Every Independent Response Is a Neurological Victory
Independence is not just a behavioural goal — it is a neurological achievement. Each time your child responds correctly without a prompt, they have activated the correct neural pathway without external triggering, demonstrated stimulus control transfer, built behavioural momentum, and reduced prompt dependency.
Wins to Celebrate That Parents Often Miss
🌟 "Today she started putting on her shoe before I pointed" — that's independent initiation
🌟 "He answered me before I finished my partial verbal" — that's anticipatory independence
🌟 "She used the visual schedule without me pointing to it" — that's self-directed visual use
🌟 "He did it the same way at school that he does at home" — that's generalisation
You are not just teaching a skill. You are building the neural infrastructure for a lifetime of independence. Every prompt you fade, every moment you wait, every time you resist doing it for them — you are the architect of their autonomy.
Red Flags That Require Professional Assessment

🚩SEEK BCBA/SPECIALIST SUPPORT IF:
• No change in prompt level for more than 6–8 consecutive sessions despite correct implementation
• Child shows increasing self-injurious behaviour (hitting, biting self) when prompts are removed
• Child's prompt dependency has intensified despite systematic fading attempts
• Skills learned in one setting completely absent in all other settings (severe generalisation failure)
• Child appears to have learned the prompt rather than the skill (responds only to very specific cue from one person)
• Parent or therapist experiencing significant distress or conflict around prompting procedures
• Child shows regression — skills previously independent now requiring prompts again

🚩SEEK MULTIDISCIPLINARY ASSESSMENT IF:
• Motor skills not developing despite physical prompting and fading (OT referral)
• Communication prompting not resulting in spontaneous communication (SLP referral)
• Behaviour during prompting sessions is escalating (ABA + clinical psychology)
• Child cannot attend to any prompt type — visual, verbal, or physical (neurological/developmental assessment)

The Full Skill Acquisition Pathway — Where You're Headed
Use your session data to identify which stage your child is currently at. Each stage has a predicted timeframe — but every child's timeline is their own. The system works; the pace varies. The Pinnacle GPT-OS® Prognosis Engine can generate skill-specific trajectory predictions based on your AbilityScore® data.
Techniques That Work Alongside Prompting
Prompting does not operate in isolation. It is most powerful when embedded within a coherent system of related techniques — each reinforcing the others to build lasting, generalisable independence.
← L-928: Shaping
The technique that builds new behaviours from scratch — foundational before prompting begins. Shaping establishes the behaviour that prompting then refines.
techniques.pinnacleblooms.org/aba-teaching/shaping-L-928
→ L-930: Reinforcement
The reward system that makes prompting work — differential reinforcement for independence. Without planned reinforcement, fading stalls.
techniques.pinnacleblooms.org/aba-teaching/reinforcement-L-930
→ L-931: Generalisation
Taking prompted skills across settings, people, and materials toward true independence. Generalisation is the finish line for every skill.
techniques.pinnacleblooms.org/aba-teaching/generalization-L-931
→ L-932: Maintenance
Keeping skills alive after prompts are fully removed — long-term independence. Maintenance planning prevents regression.
techniques.pinnacleblooms.org/aba-teaching/maintenance-L-932
